title: Boss: the control loop
summary: Three first-week tasks on a real Kubernetes cluster: a status report, a controlled rollout, and the right cluster and namespace.

steps.title: The scene
body: Your first week on the platform team. The tickets are small, but each one is a real cluster: every ticket below opens
its own one-node **Kubernetes 1.37** cluster with `kubectl`. Use `get` with `-A`, `-o jsonpath`, `--field-selector`,

steps.title: Ticket 1: a status report for the whole cluster
prompt: This terminal runs a **real one-node Kubernetes 1.37 cluster** (k3s) with `kubectl` (alias `k`). Pods run in several namespaces. For the weekly report, write into `~/answers/phases.txt` how many pods are
in each **phase** across **all** namespaces except `kube-system`, one line per phase, as `PHASE COUNT`, sorted by

checks.name: phases.txt has the right counts
checks.cmd: diff <(kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.metadata.namespace != "kube-system") | .status.phase' | sort | uniq -c | awk '{print $2, $1}') <(sed '/^$/d' ~/answers/phases.txt | tr -s ' ')
checks.fail: Not the right counts. `kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.namespace} {.status.phase}{"\n"}{end}'` lists every pod's phase.

hints: `-A` (`--all-namespaces`) lists every namespace; a pod's phase is `.status.phase` (Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed).
`--field-selector metadata.namespace!=kube-system` drops the system pods; `-o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.status.phase}{"\n"}{end}'` prints one phase per line.
solution: kubectl get pods -A --field-selector metadata.namespace!=kube-system -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.status.phase}{"\n"}{end}' | sort | uniq -c | awk '{print $2, $1}' > ~/answers/phases.txt
steps.explain: STATUS in `kubectl get pods` mixes the phase with reasons (`CrashLoopBackOff`, `Completed`); the phase itself is one of five values and is what you count and alert on. `-A`, `--field-selector` and `jsonpath` let you ask a cluster-wide question without a script, and the same jsonpath works in `kubectl wait --for=jsonpath=...`.

steps.title: Ticket 2: roll out without losing capacity
prompt: This terminal runs a **real one-node Kubernetes 1.37 cluster** (k3s) with `kubectl` (alias `k`). `checkout` runs 4 replicas and must **never drop below 4 ready pods** during a release, while
only **one** extra pod at a time may be added (the cluster is tight).
2. Roll out the new version: change the container `whoami` to run with the argument `--name=checkout-v2` (same image),
and wait for the rollout to finish.
3. Write the revision number the Deployment is now at (from `kubectl rollout history`) into `~/answers/revision.txt`.

checks.name: the new version is rolled out
checks.fail: The pods should run with `--name=checkout-v2`, all 4 updated and ready.

checks.name: revision.txt has the current revision
checks.fail: Not the current revision. `kubectl rollout history deploy/checkout` lists them; the last one is current.

hints: A change to the pod template starts a rollout: `kubectl patch deploy checkout --type=json -p '[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/args","value":["--name=checkout-v2"]}]'`.
`kubectl rollout status deploy/checkout`, then `kubectl rollout history deploy/checkout`.
steps.explain: `maxSurge` and `maxUnavailable` are the controller's budget: here it may add one pod above 4 and may never go below 4 ready, so it replaces pods one at a time, waiting for each new one to be Ready. Changing only the strategy does not start a rollout; changing the pod template does, and each one becomes a new revision (a new ReplicaSet) that `rollout undo` can go back to.

steps.title: Ticket 3: the right cluster, the right namespace
prompt: This terminal runs a **real one-node Kubernetes 1.37 cluster** (k3s) with `kubectl` (alias `k`). You have a kubeconfig in `~/.kube/config` (this terminal uses it: `kubectl config get-contexts`)
with one context, `dojo`, whose namespace is the default one. You will mostly work on the payments team's namespace.
1. Add a context named `payments` that uses the same cluster and user as `dojo`, with the namespace `payments`, and
2. Without switching contexts, write the number of Deployments in the namespace `shop` into `~/answers/shop-deploys.txt`.

checks.name: the current context is payments
checks.fail: The current context is not `payments`. `kubectl config use-context payments`.

checks.name: it targets the payments namespace on the same cluster and user
checks.fail: The `payments` context should use cluster `dojo`, user `dojo` and namespace `payments`.

checks.name: a plain kubectl get now shows the payments pods
shop-deploys.txt is right
checks.cmd: test "$(xargs < ~/answers/shop-deploys.txt)" = "$(kubectl get deploy -n shop -o name | wc -l)"
checks.fail: Not the number of Deployments in `shop`. `kubectl get deploy -n shop`: `-n` overrides the context's namespace for one command.

hints: `kubectl config set-context payments --cluster=dojo --user=dojo --namespace=payments` creates the context.
`kubectl config use-context payments` switches; `kubectl config get-contexts` marks the current one with `*`.
`kubectl get deploy -n shop -o name | wc -l` counts without switching.
solution: kubectl get deploy -n shop -o name | wc -l > ~/answers/shop-deploys.txt
steps.explain: A context is just a named (cluster, user, namespace) triple in your kubeconfig, and `kubectl` acts on the current one unless `--context` or `-n` says otherwise. Most "I deleted it in the wrong place" stories start with a forgotten current context, which is why seniors put the context in their prompt and use `-n` explicitly in scripts. Tools such as `kubectx`/`kubens` only wrap these same commands.
